title: Offered to all (Sifre Deuteronomy 343)
hookLine: midrash says God offered the Torah to other nations first
tomorrow: what did the world sound like when the voice spoke?

lines: WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.
cards: The group project gets offered around the table. Nobody wants to lead it. Then someone says fine, me, and from then on it's theirs.

A midrash in the Sifre, on Moses' last blessing, tells Sinai a little like that. Before Israel, it says, God went to other peoples and offered the Torah. Each asked the same question: what's written in it?
Each heard one command that cut against its own way of life, and said no. Then Israel was asked, and answered: we will do, and we will hear. So the answer to yesterday's question is: others.
The Torah was offered to all.

teach.b: Here's that view in full. The blessing says the LORD came from Sinai, rose from Seir and shone from mount Paran, places tied in the Torah to other peoples. The Sifre reads it as God knocking on other doors first.
Two things follow. The Torah was never a secret handed to one club; it was offered to the world. And Israel's yes was a choice, which is part of why it's worth keeping.

In tractate Shabbat, a sage named Rav Avdimi reads the verse where the people stand at the foot of the mountain, more literally under it, and pictures God holding the mountain over them like a barrel: accept, or this is your grave.
That sounds like no choice at all, and the Talmud says so out loud: then the covenant could be challenged.
Rava answers that they accepted it again, freely, in the days of Esther.
So which is it, chosen or pressed? Both sit inside the tradition, and each guards something.
The Sifre guards dignity: you said yes. The barrel guards honesty: some commitments feel bigger than you at the start, and the fully free yes can come later, when no one is holding a mountain.
A parent could put it at dinner like this: you didn't pick where you started, and you still get to choose it.

how: Jewish teaching remembers Israel's answer at Sinai, na'aseh ve-nishma, 'we will do and we will hear', and the festival of Shavuot celebrates the giving of the Torah; the midrash that it was first offered to other peoples is retold in study and sermons.

s: in the Sifre, Israel was the only people ever offered the Torah
the Sifre has God going to other peoples first; they asked what was in it and said no.
the Talmud pictures the mountain held over Israel like a barrel
Shabbat 88a, reading the people standing 'under' the mountain.
Jewish tradition has one settled view of how the Torah was accepted
the Sifre stresses choice; the barrel story stresses pressure, then a later free yes.

games.q: a friend says: 'the barrel story proves the Torah was forced, so the yes never counted.' what's the strongest case the barrel story itself makes?
o: it names the pressure honestly, then says a fully free yes came later.
it's only a playful image, so nobody should read anything into it.
it shows the people had no say in their covenant, then or later.
games.why: the Talmud admits a forced yes could be challenged, and Rava answers that they accepted it again, freely, in the days of Esther.

practice: Find a pen and a scrap of paper. Write one thing you didn't pick but are choosing now: a family, a name, a promise, a practice.
Under it, in a few words, write why you'd say yes to it today, and keep the paper somewhere you'll see it again.

wordCard.voice: Offered to all: the Sifre's telling of Sinai. The Torah held out to other peoples first, and taken up by the one that said we will do, and we will hear.

orig.note: Hebrew: we will do and we will hear (Exodus 24:7), Israel's answer at Sinai.

carryVoice: Pocket this: offered to all. A yes you chose, even second, is a yes worth keeping.

sources.ref: Sifre Deuteronomy 343 (on Deuteronomy 33:2: God offers the Torah to other peoples, who ask what is written in it and refuse)
Deuteronomy 33:2 (from Sinai, Seir and mount Paran)
Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 88a (Rav Avdimi bar Hama bar Hasa: the mountain like a barrel; Rav Acha bar Yaakov: a protest against the Torah; Rava: accepted again in the days of Ahasuerus, Esther 9:27)
